utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I return to the question of how much time should be available for the evidence-in-chief of this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we've heard submissions on this, if I may say, very adequately presented by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. We've had the opportunity of reflecting on the matter and we've made a decision. I'm not sure there's really anything you can add to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, first -- two points I'd like to clarify -- three, if I may, and I am only doing it because of my role in charge of the case as a whole and there's one thing I want to say. First of all, in case there's any ambiguity, what we're seeking is six days, not four, that is, two additional days. We hope that was clear. Second, the Prosecution's position is that it would be wrong, frankly wrong, given the quality, the integrity, and the detail of this witness to exclude any of his evidence. Third, and I think this was not available in detail last night, there is the statistics of the number of witnesses who would be saved having to give evidence, and some analysis of the material that would be lost if it was other than the full six days available for evidence. And the statistics may help the Court, and I hope they will enable you to review any decision tentatively made or provisionally made other than to grant the two additional days. Originally, we were allowed 71 witnesses for Croatia. We forecast - obviously these things are not capable of the greatest precision - that the fifth day of evidence of this witness would enable us to save eight witnesses who we otherwise had a settled intention to call; some four experts, two low-level insiders, and two verifiers of a document. The sixth day would enable us to save a further five crime-base witnesses and one journalist witness dealing with crime-base matters. Accordingly, the total potential saving for those two additional days would be some 14 witnesses, which is in the order of 20 per cent of the allocation. And in our respectful submission, it is entirely right that the witness should be heard in full. If he is not heard in full, material that will be left out would include direct contacts between the witness and other members of the joint criminal enterprise plus evidence simply not available elsewhere of the military structures of the areas of the crimes allegedly committed. In our submission, this is material that the Chamber should have, can have in the most economic form from this witness, and that it would be inappropriate or wrong to exclude. Thank you for allowing me to add to the arguments that were, as I entirely accept, fully expressed -- not fully expressed, but expressed before she had an opportunity with the team to do the research last night by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I must say that I think this part of the case has been going very slowly indeed. In twenty-plus days we've heard about 12 witnesses. And of course, it is a matter of concern as to how you're going to get through your case by the dates which we've allocated, with such adjustment as there must be for illness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I respond? Or maybe Your Honour hasn't completed what you're going to say. The suggestion that the evidence has been going slowly is one that we couldn't accept. The evidence is entirely different in character because it's so much denser in content and we have taken every available procedure to make matters go swiftly. We are, of course, bound by the decisions of the Chamber in relation to matters of 92 bis and so on, but we forecast that the very character of the evidence that is coming in at the beginning of this phase of the trial will in fact enable us to prove our case in, we hope, and realistically expect, the original overall time allocations made by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think it was the 12th of May. That day stands for the moment. We will make such adjustment as we can and we think proper for illness, but that is the date which you must have in mind, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have. And of course I will do, in respect of remaining witnesses, everything that can be done, as the whole team has been doing so far, to make use of procedural steps to abbreviate evidence. But we are bound by the Rules of the Tribunal and the practices of the Chamber. So we press you to say that it is simply inappropriate to restrict this witness's evidence and economic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's not the evidence; it's the speed with which it's being taken. It can be taken more expeditiously, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I respectfully differ from that view, and my learned colleague is, of course, master of the detail, as is the witness, and the evidence is necessarily delivered at a speed that is going to be capable of being understood and assimilated. There are other ways evidence can be given. I'm only too happy for that to be dealt with. Statements can be read, pre-read, and a witness can adopt his statement, but those are not practices that this Chamber is yet in a position to accept, and therefore we have the viva voce system of question and answer, and I would reject entirely any suggestion that my learned colleague has not been proceeding with this matter other than at a good speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not my view. Not that -- no criticism, may I say, but -- because counsel, of course, approach things in their own way, and I accept that. And counsel, as we recognise, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff considers the duty which she has to put the matter before us and also the witness on occasion replies at a bit of length. Well, we'll consider the matter and we'll reflect on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think I can see your point, but what was the base then when the Prosecution at the outset had said that it expected to conclude this witness in three days and a half and how was it changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know, until you -- until you do these things, you can never be quite sure, and of course Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff was well aware of the considerable pressure that would be on her from the Chamber to deal with matters at a particular speed. Until you actually do it in court, you can't know. Now, this witness -- and again, this is something that we have to take into account. Witnesses are not as we would like them to be; they are as they are. He's a meticulous man who gives evidence in detail, according to the process of his memory and thought processes, and there is a limit to which you can make one witness into a witness of another type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful to Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Of course, we have to remind the Chamber, we pressed you to apply the provisions of 92 bis, which would have saved many hours or days, but the Chamber took a different view. We would have preferred all the background material to have been pre-read in a way that we respectfully press on the Chamber is entirely appropriate, safe, and preserving of the accused's rights. But the Chamber took a contrary view, which we have, of course, respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm not saying that I would accede to the request, but it would seem to me that if we were to consider it favourably, we would have to hold you very strictly to the 14 witnesses whom you say you will not call. I would like to see the names of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would always hope my word in court is something that will be accepted. As to holding us to account, if that's expressed in the view that my word is accepted, then of course I have absolutely no problem with that as a proposition. I'm in a position to provide the list of the names of those who we at present regard as witnesses we would no longer seek to call. Yes, I can provide you with a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you speak into the microphone? The interpreters couldn't hear you. Witness, yesterday we spoke about the removal of Frenki and Captain Dragan from the region in August, and I would like to ask you in this context about a meeting. I would like to do that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I would be grateful if you would remind us in terms of where we are, in which paragraph, from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in paragraph 191.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, after Frenki had left the region, did you meet Mr. Stanisic in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question? Who are you referring to? Who did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I didn't get any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English channel? Can you hear the English? Yes? Could you repeat the question, please? Whom were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Jovica Stanisic, Mr. Martic, and Mr. Orlovic in August 1991 in Knin; and if so, where did you meet and what did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We did meet. It was after Frenki's removal and Captain Dragan. Jovica Stanisic arrived in Knin. I was called to come. He was there and Martic was there, in a cafe called Vrelo near Knin, and in my presence, Stanisic criticised Orlovic for the events that had occurred before that. Martic just laughed to himself. He didn't feel that the criticism was addressed to him specifically, and Orlovic as well. He accepted the criticisms that were made, but he didn't feel that they were against him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During this conversation, did Mr. Stanisic make any reference to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Oh, I beg your pardon. Yes. Yes, of course. In the course of that conversation, yes, he did say. He said, "Why are they doing the things the way they're doing?" And he was referring to Knin, what was happening in Knin, so that President Milosevic has to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, what was Stanisic's role and relationship vis-a-vis Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the executive official for Mr. Milosevic, and I saw him as the Number Two man in Slobodan Milosevic's regime. So the Number Two man, second in importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanisic say anything to this effect to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was lots of information, lots of facts pertaining to his relationship with Milosevic. A case in point, an example from Serbia's internal policy. Stanisic, for example, said at one point that Milosevic, the president, is dealing with foreign affairs and I deal internal affairs and I won the elections for him. Then there was another example with respect to involvement in Bosnia around Gorazde, in 1994, in the month of April or towards the end of April, May perhaps. He said, after Milosevic and Karadzic, with representatives of the international community agreed upon a truce, a cease of hostilities around Gorazde in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Jovica commented -- Jovica Stanisic commented on that and he said that their special units, the special police units - I think he mentioned Frenki as being at the head of those units - had made the greatest contribution in the fighting over there but that they did this sidestepping Milosevic's orders. That is to say, there weren't any orders and as the president, he did not know about that. But he said it in such a way as to imply -- he wanted actually to conceal Milosevic's role in those events. He was an executor and a protector of Milosevic, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did he make this remark of this, or these special units in Gorazde? To which time period did he refer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This referred to the period of March/April 1994, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have mentioned several times Mr. Martic. You have also referred to the support that he received from Serbia. Was Mr. Martic loyal to Mr. Milosevic? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic acknowledge his loyalty publicly during the election campaign that he held in 1993/1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, publicly. During the election campaign and after the campaign as well, he said that he would be the provisional president of Krajina, and once -- that he would be only the provisional president and that he would hand over the baton to Slobodan Milosevic, the relay baton, sort of, hand over the office. And people made jokes about that in Knin, saying that he would hand over his police baton to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion with Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Martic in August 1991 in relation to the position of the TO commander in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I did have that conversation in Mr. Milosevic's offices. I was invited to go to Milosevic's offices and I met Martic there. Martic was already at Milosevic's. And without any great introduction, Milosevic said the following: He said, "Let Mile be the commander of the Territorial Defence," and he was thinking about Mile Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Martic, who was present there, and he repeated that. I think that the conversation went on for about two hours. Milosevic kept repeating that sentence. And I think he repeated it countless times; at least, many, many times, just that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you object against Martic being the TO commander; and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I did object, and that is why Milosevic kept repeating that particular sentence, because he felt that I was opposed. I asked for some objective reasons, quite simply. I said, "Well, he's a policeman. He can't -- you can't have a policeman command the Territorial Defence. You would need a general, the rank of general or colonel or somebody who has been trained in the National Defence School and has the rank of general. It's a professional post and he needs to have a staff of at least ten persons." So my objections went along those lines and I objected to his proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go into open session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness the Exhibit tab 64 in Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, it's an appointment of Milan Martic to the position of deputy commander of the TO of the SAO Krajina. Why was he appointed into this position, and what competence did go along with this position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was appointed because he was the Minister of the Interior, and in that way the police in Krajina were incorporated into the new system and placed under the authority of the government of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday we spoke about a report. It was an exhibit, tab 67, a report on the military activities in the region in August 1991. This report that also went to Frenki. And in this report, there was mentioned a ceasefire, an order that Mile Martic gave regarding a ceasefire. Was a ceasefire actually agreed upon on the 6th of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Despite the ceasefire, was Kijevo attacked in August 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of August, it was attacked, yes. And before that, Milan Martic laid down an ultimatum to the police and inhabitants of Kijevo, telling them to leave Kijevo, on the 18th of August, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness tab 68 from Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is that the ceasefire -- the ultimatum that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you got information on this ultimatum, what was your reaction to it? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt of this ultimatum from the media, and I issued a denial through the media, saying that the armed forces of SAO Krajina would not violate the ceasefire. I think it was the next day after I had heard about the ultimatum on the media, so it was the 19th or the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And your denial, was it made publicly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, publicly. It was in the press. The press carried it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did this -- did your denial, did it cause a reaction by Martic, the JNA, or the Belgrade authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, with the exception of the fact that they were more intolerant towards me personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you called to go to Belgrade on the 25th of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was invited to go to Belgrade and to report to President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you talk about on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About two things: First of all, when I arrived, President Milosevic asked me how things were down there in Knin, and I said that there were problems, that the Croatian police from Sinj had gone there to mistreat the population in the village of Otisic and that there was no JNA there to protect them. And he said, "Hasn't that already been settled?" And I said, "I don't know." After the meeting I heard -- it was reported to me, I was informed that that morning that the JNA and all armed formations under its control had attacked Kijevo and the region. And then he asked me about General Spiro Nikolic. I couldn't say anything for or against that man who was the commander of the Knin Corps. Then he said, "Frenki needs to be down there in Krajina. He needs to go back there. He's a good man, Frenki's good." That was his comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were away from Knin in this conversation that you just had, was it on that exact day Kijevo attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was attacked on that day, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which forces were involved in this attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA corps from Knin, units of the Krajina police, and the local TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did you see anything to this effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, I passed through the area and I saw the commander of the Knin brigade, Colonel Djukic, and officers from his group. And he said that the chief of staff of the corps, Ratko Mladic, was in front of him, going towards Otisic. I saw a tank column of which Djukic was in command, and this was in front of Vrljika. I saw a unit of TO of Cetine on the edges of the village of Cetine, towards Vrljika. And they told me that the police had been there too, Martic and Milenko Zelenbaba. And this was shown on Belgrade television as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see that on Belgrade television, Martic in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Belgrade television showed two scenes from Kijevo. One was Martic and Zelenbaba removing the Croatian flag from the police station and embracing each other, and the other was Vesna Jugovic, a reporter of Belgrade television, interviewing a soldier of the JNA on the road through the village of Kijevo. That is, a talk between him and an old man from Kijevo, an old Croat who had stayed behind. And this soldier asked him the following: "Did you kill my grandfather in 1941?" And the man says, "I did not."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Let me stop you there. Witness, you said that you came through this region a day later. What did Kijevo look like? Did you see any Croats? Was it intact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place was deserted. The inhabitants could not be seen. It had been destroyed by artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On that day, did you see Mr. Mladic actually in the field? On this day or the next days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the next day or two, after I was again passing along that road, that is, through Vrljika.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was he doing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was returning from Otisic. He was accompanying a group of representatives of the Croatian authorities from Sinj and Split. He was accompanying them to Vrljika, which was under his administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, did he actually participate in fighting activities on the ground? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He participated and he was in command. The reporters even said that he was in the front lines and that he de-mined obstacles and he appeared on all parts of the front suddenly, on his own, with groups. And I remember that when the new Corps Commander arrived, General Vukovic, and Mladic asked him to report to him where the corps units were deployed. Then Mladic showed on the map that there were small groups of units of the corps on various parts of the front in the area of northern Dalmatia. And then the general said, "Where is the corps?" But that is the way Mladic commanded the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that Mladic commanded the corps. Was he the Corps Commander or what was his position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladic, from the summer and through the autumn of 1991, he was Chief of Staff of the corps. For a time, that is, in September, when Spiro Nikolic, the previous general, was moved to another position before Vukovic arrived, he was the most senior officer. In 1992, he was for a time the Corps Commander, that is, Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to go into private session again for the next meeting with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Milosevic in September 1991 in relation to a TO commander for the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around the 12th of September, 1991, in connection with the TO staff. Officers for the TO staff of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have a proposal to make as to the new TO commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Borivoj Rasuo and Zoran Kalicanin, a man from the information service of the JNA. They recommended to me Radosav Maksic, a colonel that I met on that occasion, and who had volunteered to go together with ten other officers and form the Main Staff of the TO SAO Krajina. But Maksic wanted me to seek approval from Milosevic for him to be discharged as he was in active service in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Milosevic's position when you informed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he would do what is necessary for them to come. And he was in a very good mood then. That is when I met Jovica Stanisic, in his offices; not in the same room, but the room next to his. That was when he was in the best mood, compared to all the other encounters I had with him. He even shared his lunch with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean Mr. Milosevic agreed to your proposal to appoint Maksic as the TO commander? What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That's right. They will come -- he'll come."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you mentioned Mr. Stanisic, that you saw him also on that day. What was his contact -- what was your contact with him? How did that come about and what did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I entered into the study of President Milosevic, the secretary said that the president was having a break, that he was having lunch, and that I should wait in the room next to hers, or the one next to it, towards the corner. And I went inside, and Jovica Stanisic was standing behind the desk, and there was a military map in front of him with the lines drawn in of the deployment of the army. He just showed me with his eyes that I should look at the map. I looked, and then he took me to the next room. This was a semi-oval room on the corner. He closed the door and he said, "This is the room for reporting." And when I went back, the secretary said, "You can go in, the president will receive you." And the president received me, though he hadn't finished his lunch. He shared his lunch with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you here. What did you see on the map that Mr. Stanisic was dealing with? Do you recall what kind of a map or what kind of a region it dealt with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a military topographical map, and the scale, I think, was about 1:50.000 or 1:100.000. And it had a red line drawn on it in the area of Northern Dalmatia. I am familiar with the area, the topography of the area, and I knew that the army was there. And the line indicated the positions of the army, across the Perucac Lake, the Svilaja mountain, Petrova Polje, Cikova, and the surroundings of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the -- did Colonel Maksic actually arrive, and his ten officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some ten days went by and they didn't arrive, and I called President Milosevic's secretary on the phone and I asked for the president, and she said he wasn't there but she would connect me to him. And I asked him, "What about the officers?" And he said, "They're coming tomorrow." They didn't come tomorrow, but they came five or six or seven days later. But not ten officers; Maksic and another two.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they arrive, and what position did they take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Dusan Kasum came as the chief of staff of the TO SAO Krajina; Colonel Vuletic, as the chief of communications; and Colonel Maksic, as the operative chief. They came to Martic's at the Knin fortress, and they called me to come there and I arrived and I saw only three of them, and they just shrugged their shoulders. And I asked, "Is Martic the commander?" And he said, "Call General Simovic." He was the Minister of Defence of Serbia. And I called him and I asked, "Is Maksic the commander of the TO staff of SAO Krajina?" And he said, "We have designated General Djujic." And he gave an explanation for Martic, an excuse why he couldn't hold that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what was the reason why General Djujic was supposed to take the position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simovic said that Maksic was an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher I would like just to put to you the decisions made in this regard. It's tab 69, appointment of General Djujic, Maksic, Kasum and Vuletic; tab 70, appointment Colonel Djujic; tab 71, appointment Maksic; tab 72, order to relieve Djujic; tab 46 -- sorry, 49.6 is a decision to appoint Colonel Tabok; and tab 51.1 and 50.2, decisions to relieve Dusan Starevic from -- and Velibor Matijasevic from their positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are these decisions taken in relation to the TO command and the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually, in the Krajina, make the substantial decisions, or are these just the official documents confirming decisions taken by others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were formal, legal decisions confirming decisions taken by the competent authorities in Belgrade, in this case, the General Staff and the Secretary of National Defence. These two documents about Matijasevic and Starevic, they are not directly linked to the Main Staff of the TO but rather linked to the obstruction of the Assembly, which was done by a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. parallel structure with a view to influencing negotiations in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, those TO commanders that were then appointed, were they controlled by the politicians in the Krajina? Did they report to the politicians in the Krajina or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not. They themselves didn't establish control over the unified TO of SAO Krajina, but it remained subordinated to the competent units of the JNA, according to various regions, and they themselves were subordinated to the JNA command.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have to put to you just another document in this context, and it's tab 73 of the Exhibit 352. This is an order -- a certificate, actually, by the SFRY Presidency signed by Vice-President Branko Kostic and Colonel Milo Kostic, in relation to promotion of Colonel Kasum to the Chief of Staff of the TO Defence in April 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's promoted to the rank of general, but he was previously appointed to the Chief of Staff of the TO of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean afterwards - we are talking now about April 1992 - this relationship between the TO --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This relationship of the TO staff, the officers there, and the JNA, or VJ, as it later was called, remained the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It remained the same until August 1995. Virtually, it was Slobodan Milosevic who appointed the commanders of the Serbian army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to the TO in the Krajina, did you have opportunity to review, during your conversations here in The Hague, a lot of documents that related to appointments, related to organisation of units? Did you review these documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you authenticate all these documents? Could you -- did you know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not want to put all these documents to the witness. I just want to read to you, and for the record, which documents the witness reviewed and confirmed as being made by the authorities there. And it's actually all from the Exhibit 352, and it is tabs 114, 115, 117 to 119, 121 to 141, 145, 148, 150, 151. These are the documents that I would like to refer to in this regard. It's all appointments and all formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These decisions taken, were they respected by the JNA and the Martic police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some decisions, yes; some, no. The decisions relating to active-duty officers in their role were respected. A part of the decisions that were passed in July, August, and September of 1991 were not respected.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, 151 was dropped; yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, Your Honour. I just got the note from my colleague here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to the problems that arose between decisions on TO from the local politicians and in relation to the JNA ignoring parts of them, did you have a meeting with General Vukovic and General Djujic in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, around the 10th of October, 1991, in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you talk about, and what was the result of these talks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djujic initiated the meeting with General Vukovic that we should address the question of competence over the TO; which would be the competent command? Would it be the corps command of the JNA or the staff of the TO by SAO Krajina? General Vukovic said that he was not competent and that, in this connection, General Adzic should be contacted in the General Staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you do that? Did you contact General Adzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was received by General Adzic, not in the command of the General Staff but in another military institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what did you discuss with him, and what was the result of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the main topics: The outcome was that nothing would be changed, that the competence of the command of the JNA remained, that that is how it was envisaged in the system and that is how it would remain. Then there were other things discussed, and I took note of them in my notebook that I took with me, as a memo. The issues that Djujic said I should address with Adzic regarding supplies, the status of the people in the TO, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Adzic -- General Adzic's position to demands that you made? How did he react to this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the effect that there would be no problems. He wasn't very specific about it. That things would be resolved, words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Open session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness the document tab 74 of Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, what kind of a document is this and who prepared it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was compiled in the Main Staff of the TO of SAO Krajina, and it was a report, in fact, on the situation in the SAO TO of the Krajina in 1991, October.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: For whom was this prepared and to whom was this given?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was prepared for the Prime Minister, first and foremost, and then it was drafted for the General Staff of the JNA, to be handed on to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it handed to General Adzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that exactly, but he did receive information about these issues, as we had discussed them previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those matters raised here, the needs of the TO, were these the matters that were discussed with General Adzic on the occasion that you described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I would like now to move on to discussions held about the Carrington plan and the future Yugoslavia. What were the proposals for the Krajina? What were the proposals for the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Lord Carrington's general plan, proposals were made for three types of relationships amongst the republics of the former Yugoslavia. For areas inhabited in individual republics with ethnic communities having certain characteristics, it was provided that they should be granted a special territorial status, and this referred to Krajina as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was -- was there stated a certain autonomy within the Croatian context?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Territorial autonomy within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you take part in several -- actually, in three negotiations with Mr. Wijnaendts, the Dutch ambassador, in relation to the Carrington plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Every time before the plenary meetings would take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And before you went to these negotiations with Mr. Wijnaendts, did you meet Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade before you went there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always. That's right. Always before that, there would be a meeting with President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you go there to get instructions, or why did you meet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were invited to go to Belgrade to receive instructions as to what stand to take.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you go there for the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the 13th of October, 12th or 13th. But anyway, before the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what instruction did you get?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instructions were that the plan was a good one for us. Not to accept it directly, but the suggestion was that, in general terms, the plan was a good one for us. That was from President Milosevic and a few people that he had called in to his offices to explain the plan to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who explained the plan to you? Were these officials from the Belgrade government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was an advisor to President Milosevic, Mr. Kutlesic. The others were people with whom President Milosevic associated. They were professors, university professors Smilja Avramov, Ratko Markovic, Kosta Mihajlovic, Vasilije Krestic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That first time when you had this meeting in Belgrade, did anything happen? Did anything happen in Knin that alerted you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. What happened was that after we started off towards Belgrade -- two things actually happened. Velibor Matijasevic, president of the Assembly of the SAO Krajina, convened an Assembly meeting, asking for a report on the work of the government of SAO Krajina. And the other thing that happened, the second thing - and Ljubica Solaja conveyed this to me - that in the police station in Knin, Frenki was informing or inciting the Serbs present in the police station that Babic was a traitor. So that was before my departure. During the meeting with Milosevic, I was under this pressure that I had to go to The Hague -- I apologise, to Paris for a meeting with Wijnaendts, and that I was required to give a report to the Assembly. And at one point, I said -- and Milosevic was standing there by the table or walking around the table while we were sitting down, I said, "I can't be in Paris and in Knin at the same time, simultaneously." And he said to me, "I know nothing about that." I said, "Well, Jovica does," and I meant Jovica Stanisic. "He knows about it." And Milosevic left the room, and a little while later I was told that the Assembly had been cancelled, that Matijasevic had in fact cancelled the Assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So you went to Paris, and what position did you take there? Did you accept the plan or speak in favour of the plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't, and neither did the other members of the delegation. They didn't adopt the plan. They didn't come out in favour of the plan. But we expressed our readiness to continue discussing the plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: After you returned to -- from Paris, did you report about the negotiations to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milosevic did receive information about the negotiations because we went to see him once again before we left for the 18th, the second meeting. And on that occasion, I remember that he was very energetic in his reactions towards me. He said, "Accept it and let's get this over with. Serbia has the chance of bringing -- having a state, being a state, and everything else will be engulfed in darkness." But I didn't accept that proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What does that mean? What exactly did he say in relation to Serbia has a chance of having a state, or being a state? What does that relate to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To survive as a state, and all the rest would become chaotic, one general state of chaos, war or whatever. And that of all the Yugoslav republics on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, it had the chance of obtaining status -- the status of a state, that all the rest would be engulfed in darkness and that they would become colonies of the powers that be. Something along those lines, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that refer to Croatia and Slovenia and Bosnia? Did he say anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said all that, except Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on this second meeting with Wijnaendts, what position did you take there? Did you accept the plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not following this story. He's told by Mr. Milosevic to accept the plan. But it now seems he doesn't accept the plan. And I just don't follow what's being said here at all. Perhaps he could explain his position and how this all comes about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, can you explain Mr. Milosevic's position when you came there for the second time to, as you say, get directives? What was Mr. Milosevic's position in relation to the Carrington plan, and what did you afterwards then do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of President Milosevic was that we should accept the plan, the portion relating to us, which means special status within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And were you prepared to do that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were not prepared at that point in time to accept that. We understood that President Milosevic wanted to pull himself out of the war and leave us to the Croats to take their revenge on us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were in Paris after this second meeting with Wijnaendts, did you make a public statement as to your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second meeting took place in The Hague, at the Foreign Ministry in The Hague, and I did make several statements. One was to the effect that I was representing the SAO Krajina and the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina there, which was not quite proper and was not what had been agreed upon at the meeting itself. And we did not accept the plan on that occasion either. The proposal at that time was in fact - that is to say, Ambassador Wijnaendts' - that we look into the status of the Tyrol in Italy and in that way to see whether that could be a possible model for Krajina within Croatia, to follow the Tyrolean model.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you meet Mr. Milosevic afterwards, after this second meeting with Wijnaendts? Did you have a conversation with him then again, in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. On the 20th of October and on the 23rd, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. think it was, October. The first time was in his offices and the second time in the Palace of the Federation in New Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's speak about the meeting on the 20th of October. What was the purpose of the meeting, and what was said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was for him to tell me that I was supposed to go to Banja Luka, to a meeting there with Radovan Karadzic - Karadzic had organised a meeting there - to reject Carrington's plan. That means that the representatives of the Serbs from Bosnia and SAO Krajina, Western Slavonia, should reject the plan, and at the same time -- I don't know whether this was his intention previously, but he did tell me, he swore, Momir Bulatovic, in very explicit terms, said he was a traitor and said he had his people there, a party there, who would replace him and bring him to order, Momir Bulatovic, that is, in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What had Momir Bulatovic done that Mr. Milosevic was angry about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the second plenary conference in The Hague, Bulatovic accepted Carrington's plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you just told us that Mr. Milosevic had given you, actually, the directive to accept the Carrington plan. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was quite a different reaction from the previous two times. Whether the cause of that was that the plan looked at the status of Kosovo, as it had in 1974, or whether it was what was criticised, that Milosevic criticised and everybody around him, and that Yugoslavia and the concept of Yugoslavia was being denied in that way, and the preservation of that part of Yugoslavia that he came out in favour of. So these were two things that they put forward in public, publicly, as reasons for rejecting the Carrington plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So the proposal at that time was different from the proposal that Mr. Milosevic had asked you to accept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, and that was the same thing on the 23rd, when he proposed that for the upcoming meeting with Wijnaendts this be done, when he put forward four points for our position in the Palace of the Federation, the meeting that we attended together at the Federation Palace building in the New Belgrade district of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is now the meeting -- you're referring to the meeting on the 23rd of October?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who was present during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Present were many people; representatives of Serbia, Montenegro, and the Serb people from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the SAO Krajina, Western and Eastern Slavonia. Which means Slobodan Milosevic, the president of the Assembly of Serbia; academician Kanazir, president of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences; members of the Presidency, Branko Kostic, Jovic and the rest, Karadzic, his people from Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of that meeting on the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The outcome of the meeting was that Branko Kostic, who chaired the meeting, counted that there were more people in Yugoslavia in favour of Yugoslavia. He calculated 10 per cent more and that it was noted that as the majority were in favour of Yugoslavia, that Yugoslavia should remain and that that was the position that should be put forward at The Hague conference with respect to Lord Carrington's plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic give you a special instruction on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that Wijnaendts was expecting me in Paris -- I beg your pardon? Yes, in Paris, that's right, for the third time, and he gave me four items, four points to discuss, my positions to be advocated there by me. The first was a special status for the SAO Krajina and the other three points I can't remember now. I wasn't -- I was a bit wary and I asked where special status, and he said on Yugoslav territory, and he gave me this piece of paper. And the paper is -- remained with Borivoje Rasuo, I think. I took the paper from him. And at the conference in Paris, in fact, Ambassador Wijnaendts -- as soon as we began, I didn't expound my position, but he said, "Mr. Babic, we can accept everything." That's what he said, "And we can accept point 1, item 1," and I assumed that Milosevic had already informed them of our so-called positions. Actually, he instructed us in those positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This paper that you got from Mr. Milosevic, was it made by him? Was it in handwriting? What kind of a paper was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was typed out. Four items typed out, and in hand he had added, "On Yugoslav territory."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean special status on Yugoslav territory? Is that what he suggested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it meant, although it could have been interpreted otherwise as well. I wasn't quite clear on what it actually meant, and I couldn't take it, and I didn't want to go to Paris. I went to Knin and I said I was ill.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you nevertheless go to Paris, and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He called me up on the telephone again several days later. That was around the 28th or 29th of October. And he said, "What's happening to you? What's up with you?" And I said I was ill and he said, "I don't believe doctors who are ill themselves. Go on, Wijnaendts is waiting for you," he said. And I went.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went by plane. We flew there. Small planes, first and second occasion, once owned by the federal government, and the second time it was a small military plane and the pilots were soldiers and it left from the military airport of Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did you meet Mr. Milosevic end of November/beginning of December 1991 regarding the Vance plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, around the 23rd of November, that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At that time, was the Vance plan already accepted by Mr. Milosevic, Kadijevic, and Tudjman? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. It had already been accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you talk with Mr. Milosevic about it then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milosevic set out the basic concepts of the plan that had been accepted and he showed a map and indicated the territories. He showed me a map, and in yellow -- yellow marked the municipalities in Croatia and the territories of the municipalities to which the plan referred. These areas were marked in in yellow. But parts of the municipalities were not highlighted in yellow. The municipalities, or one of the municipalities which had -- was joined to SAO Krajina in Banija, Lika, and Kordun. And I said that, but he didn't want to discuss this issue, this point, with me. He just said, "Go down there and talk to the international delegation of the United Nations" which was there in the salon adjoined to his offices one floor below, and I found Ratko Jovanovic there and he interpreted for me. He interpreted the conversation I had with the representatives of the Security Council of the United Nations. And they put forward this same concept for the plan that I had heard earlier on from him. And already at that time, I began making some remarks of my own, and the positions that I stood by, and I did this over the next two months or more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic ask you to accept the Vance plan when you met him on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He wanted us to say that we accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you did -- did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you request amendments; and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I did request amendments. I asked that the JNA remain in Krajina, that the peace forces be deployed along the line of conflict between the two warring sides, the Serbian and Croatian side. It was called the green line, modelled upon the Cyprus model. And I asked that the laws of Croatia not be applied to the SAO Krajina territory and that the Territorial Defence of SAO Krajina not be disbanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just remind us, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Perhaps you can do this through the witness shortly -- the basis of the plan, and then we can find out why the witness took the view which he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, what was the main point in relation to the Vance plan? You have already mentioned the territories that were specially marked in a map. What was supposed to become out of these territories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a provisional plan through which demilitarisation of those areas was to be conducted, and this was marked as Krajina Sector West and Sector East, and later on they were referred to as Sector East, Sector North, Sector South and Sector West; and the JNA was to withdraw from those areas and that all the units remaining, the armed forces remaining in the area, should be disbanded, including the Territorial Defence units; and that all volunteer units should be withdrawn outside the territory of Krajina, those who had come in from outside into the territory; and that all that should remain of the armed formations in the area in all three, or rather, four areas, sectors, should be the police, with their arms at their waists, that is to say, without any long-barrelled weapons, and that it should be proportionate to the population structure before the conflict - police with sidearms - until a political solution for the area was found. And in item 1, point 1, it was stated that there were nine regions to which the plan referred. They were different areas within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm sorry to have to interrupt you once again, but I have become very tired reading from the transcript. I was saying, it's very tiring for me to have to read from the transcript what this witness is saying, because I cannot hear the witness at all. He has turned towards that side over there and is speaking into his beard. The interpreters can hear him because he has a special microphone for the interpreters, but he has no microphone for the Serbian language because he has been granted voice distortion. I understand that. But could he please be asked to speak louder? And I believe that Mr. Tapuskovic probably can't hear him either, but he doesn't dare complain. He is reluctant to complain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If Mr. Tapuskovic wanted to complain, he would. No doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did complain on one occasion, but I didn't want to tire you with my complaints. If you remember, the day before yesterday I said that I cannot hear the witness at all, and I complained on the first day. When he is going into explanations in private session, he speaks louder, but when he's explaining matters in open session, it is very difficult to understand what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note Mr. Mueller is on his feet. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just wanted to inform you that my headphones are absolutely impeccable, means to say that I hear the voice of the witness very clearly, as I do the English translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've got comments all around. I think we're going to adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we in closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm going to speak to the witness. You hear what's said, Mr. Witness MILAN BABIC. One of the problems is that you're giving a great deal of evidence, and it's important that everybody follows it and understands it and takes it in, and it's rather difficult to do that if there's so much of it, and some of it, as you've been asked, is in some detail. It would help, it may help, if you would speak into the microphone, as you've been doing, keep your voice louder, and also if you would kindly, when you're giving your answers, perhaps face us, the Bench, so that your voice may be heard elsewhere, yes, rather than the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I have a comment to make. Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you can hear the witness saying in Serbian, why don't you use the headphone? I'm saying this once again. You can follow very easily. And the second point is that we are going into private session so often, and if you have -- find some difficulty in following the witnesses, why don't you let your associate come in the courtroom and assist you in that aspect? I'm raising these issues while we are in private session, and consider this matter later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand, Mr. Kwon, how somebody could help me hear better. My associate can't help me hear better if I don't hear something. For example, I just had a technical remark, saying that I can't hear what the witness is saying. Otherwise, let me say that I never mentioned at all that Mr. Mueller couldn't hear, so I do believe that Mr. Mueller can hear very well. I never said that. I was just making the remark that I myself could not hear properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go into open session for one matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we've considered the application which you and Mr. Nice make. We will grant it. You will have the six days. But we will expect the list of 14 witnesses within seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We actually have identified the 14 witnesses, and we can provide it, actually, in one day. Tomorrow you will have your list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. Yes. Do we need to go back into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We can stay in open session, and I would like to clarify a few points in relation to the Vance plan, to make it perfectly clear what the provisions were, the suggestions were. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, did the Vance plan foresee the re-integration of the three SAOs into the Republic of Croatia within certain time periods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan didn't address that directly, except in the introduction, which referred to areas that were in Croatia. That is all that it said. The plan did not address the political solution. It explicitly said that a political solution would be found later. "Until a political solution is found." So the plan refers to a period until a political solution is found, except in the first paragraph, which said what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the provision was demilitarisation of the -- all three SAOs, with only a police force remaining, with the weapons that a police force usually have. Was that what you referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That was the substance of the plan; the demilitarisation of those regions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the plan foresee the arrival of UN troops, and where would the UN troops be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The plan did envisage, after the demilitarisation, the deployment of peace forces of the United Nations across the territory within the territory of those regions, and those forces would control roads, checkpoints, the entries and exits from the regions. They would check that no weapons were being introduced or carried within those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, do we have the document among our binders, the Carrington plans and Vance plans? If you assist us later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not aware of this. I think we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can get a copy. If we can, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if I understood you, your concerns, some of the Serb-controlled areas were not included in this zone that UN troops would supervise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was there a provision also in the Vance plan regarding the return of displaced persons into this territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the objectives of the international mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there also a provision in the Vance plan regarding joint police forces of Croats and Serbs within that territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, it would be in proportion to the ethnic composition of the population prior to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, at that time when the Vance plan was discussed, and you said it took almost two months to discuss this, the pros and the cons, did the -- was the RSK, the Republic of Serbian Krajina, established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 19th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness tab 68 of Exhibit 351, just to have a look at it, sir, not to discuss the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is this the constitution and constitutional law on implementation of the RSK of 19 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why was the RSK formed at that time? What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international conference in The Hague had stated that it would recognise all the republics of the former Yugoslavia that requested recognition. That virtually meant that the former Yugoslavia had disintegrated, as was stated by the Badinter Commission named by the conference. That was one of the reasons why a part of the territory of the former Yugoslavia, that is, the SAO Krajina, proclaimed itself a republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Republic of Serbian Krajina actually request international recognition?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in this context I would like to put to the witness tab 71.1 and 71.2 of the binder --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- Exhibit 351.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are these the two letters to the international officials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were you recognised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The territory of the RSK, was that identical with the SAO Krajina territory, or did that include all three SAOs at that time, on the 19th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of December, the SAO Krajina became the Republic of Serbian Krajina. On that day, the Assembly of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem proclaimed unification with the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and two days later, the Assembly of SAO Western Slavonia also proclaimed its unification with Krajina. But until the 26th of February, 1992, they were not united. All three regions on that date united, and that was when the unified Republic of Serbian Krajina was constituted, covering all three regions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have talked about the Vance plan and what the provisions were, and in relation to demilitarisation of this region, did you in the Krajina oppose that? I do not mean you personally, but the politicians in the Krajina. Did you oppose the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Vance plan covered a period of six months, upon which there would be a discussion as to whether it should be extended or not, and under those conditions, Krajina would be demilitarised, Croatia would not, and Krajina would have to face the Republic of Croatia imposing a political solution to Krajina by force of arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have any -- did you object also against the arrival of the UN troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the concept of their arrival. We didn't oppose their coming but the way in which they were to come. The deployment was envisaged according to the so-called green line, based on the Cypriot model.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant separation of the warring parties, that is, the Croatian and the Serbian side, and not demilitarisation of the area as a whole. And that is the amendment to the Vance plan that was requested. It was accepted in principle, but this modification was requested regarding certain elements of the plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there an option? Was that an option, to get a modification of the Vance plan, or was that out of question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was an option, and some provisions were modified. Regarding the initial deployment for a period of six months, and then it was extended to one year by the Security Council, the Secretary-General of the UN, in his report to the Security Council, made such a proposal, and that was accepted, and that is that Croatian laws should not apply to those territories but the laws in force at the time. There was also a discussion that the Territorial Defence should remain, that the possibility should be given that it should be incorporated into the police without long weapons, long barrels, but this was not resolved. There was just the discussion about it. So some elements were modified.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that for about two months the Krajina Serbs opposed the Vance plan, and did all of them oppose the Vance plan, or was there a split within the Krajina politicians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first they were all opposed, and gradually, more and more politicians accepted the plan fully and unconditionally in the way that President Milosevic had accepted it. And finally, the president of the Republic and the government and part of the Assembly continued to oppose it, requesting modifications of the plan, and a part of the Assembly and the politicians in Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem and part of the Assembly of SAO Krajina and some politicians accepted the plan. And the Assembly, which met in Glina on the 9th of February, 1992, approved the plan after the pressure that came from President Milosevic, the Presidency of Yugoslavia, the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, the media campaign, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to request private session to go into some details on the meetings in relation to the Vance plan.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did you attend a meeting with Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Koljevic on this issue on the 23rd of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. On that date, when there was an election of the government of Serbia, in the office of President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Without going into many details of this discussion, what was the position taken by you and by Milosevic, Karadzic, and Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I upheld the same position. That meant the plan, with modifications. Milosevic requested that I accept it fully and unconditionally and that -- make a statement to that effect for the public. Karadzic also emphatically requested that I accept the plan without any changes, as did Koljevic. Finally, Milosevic gave me a piece of paper and a pen and said, "Go to the next room and write out an announcement." I went there and wrote an announcement on one page, presenting all my positions. He took the pen and said, "I won't cross anything out, but I will underline what you need to leave out." And he underlined all the things regarding modifications of the plan, which I should leave out. I expressed my opposition, and he said, "This must go to the Assembly meeting. Radovan Bojovic [as interpreted] will be the Prime Minister of the new government, and let him help you." And when he left, Karadzic again started persuading me to accept it. I said, "Come on Radovan, let's talk about Bosnia for a moment." He went silent, and I left and made a public announcement in the way that I had drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me clarify. I find in the transcript a remark that you said Radovan Bojovic will be the Prime Minister of the government. I don't understand the context.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radoman Bozovic, Radoman Bozovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What does it have to do with the Vance plan and the discussion that you had with Mr. Milosevic and Karadzic and Koljevic? I don't understand the context. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radoman Bozovic and the members of the new government of Serbia were to be sworn in at the Assembly meeting, and that was the reason why he had to leave his room and cross over to the building of the Serbian Assembly. And as he was leaving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's difficult for us to understand the context. What was the point of this remark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point -- Your Honour, are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The context was the following: After Milosevic having underlined in my statement what I should leave out, he left the meeting because of the reason I just gave. He left the meeting, with me, Karadzic, and Koljevic, to go to the building across the road. And he said I should continue discussing it with Karadzic and Koljevic. And the words he uttered were, "Let Radovan help you to draft another statement."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That's understood now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also discuss the Vance plan with General Adzic, in particular, your concerns for the safety of the Serbs in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
